book: Nancy Caroline · Chapter 11 · Research and Quality
title: Reading Research: Study Designs, Bias and P Values
next: Chapter 11, Lesson 2: Using evidence, quality improvement and patient safety

slides.title: Today's lesson
slides.body:
As an EMR you already follow protocols that were built on research. Now, as a PCP, you need to read that research yourself:

  1. Why paramedic care must rest on evidence, not tradition
  2. Tell the main study designs apart, quickly
  3. Judge a result: bias, chance, and what a P value really means

Textbook: Chapter 11, PDF pages 800–835
slides.say: Welcome back. Today there are no new drugs or skills, but this chapter shapes every protocol you use. As an EMR you could follow a protocol without asking where it came from. This chapter uses the word paramedic for primary, advanced and critical care paramedics, so it's written for you now. And COPR, which runs your PCP written exam, names using evidence as a key pillar of paramedic competence. Today we'll cover three things: why care must rest on evidence, how to tell study designs apart, and how to judge a result, including bias, chance, and P values.
slides.sayZh: 欢迎回来。今天没有新药，也没有新技能，但这一章决定了你用的每一条流程。当 EMR 的时候，你可以照着流程做，不必追问它从哪里来。这一章里的 paramedic 指初级、高级和重症救护员，所以现在它是写给你的。负责你 PCP 笔试的 COPR，也把运用证据列为救护员能力的关键支柱之一。今天讲三件事：为什么照护必须以证据为依据；怎样分辨研究设计；怎样判断一个结果，包括偏倚、偶然和 P 值。

slides.title: Why evidence beats tradition
slides.body:
Best available evidence, not habit or authority

  • MAST: longer scene times, lower survival (1980s study)
  • Routine IV lidocaine in heart attacks caused some fatal rhythms
  • Intubation: harmful in children and some adults, such as TBI
  • Evidence + your expertise + experience = best care
slides.say: Things that seem obviously helpful can turn out to be harmful. Crews once put inflatable antishock trousers, called MAST, on hypotensive trauma patients, until a study in the nineteen-eighties found longer scene times and lower survival. Lidocaine was once given routinely by IV in heart attacks to prevent bad rhythms, but it caused some fatal ones. Even intubation, long the gold standard, has been linked to harm in children and some adults, such as those with a traumatic brain injury. Experience matters, but it can mislead. Best care combines evidence with your expertise and experience.
slides.sayZh: 看起来明明有用的做法，后来可能被证明有害。救护人员曾给低血压的创伤病人穿充气抗休克裤，也就是 MAST，直到二十世纪八十年代的一项研究发现，用了它现场时间更长、生存率更低。利多卡因曾在心梗时常规静脉给，想预防心律失常，却引起了一些致命心律。就连长期被视为金标准的气管插管，也被发现对儿童和部分成人有害，比如颅脑外伤病人。经验重要，但可能误导人。最好的照护，是把证据和你的专长、经验结合起来。

slides.title: Internal vs external validity
slides.body:
A study measures a sample, then infers what is true for everyone.

Internal validityExternal validity
Can I trust the result?Does it apply beyond the sample?
Threats: bias, confoundingThreats: a narrow or different population

Researchers often trade one for the other to make a study possible.
slides.say: Every study looks at a sample, a small group, then makes an inference, which means a conclusion, about everyone. To decide whether that conclusion holds, ask two questions. First, internal validity: can I trust this result, or could bias or confounding explain it? Second, external validity: does the result apply outside the study group, for example to my patients on the road? A trial done only in a hospital emergency department may be well run, yet not fit prehospital care. Researchers often trade one for the other to make a study possible.
slides.sayZh: 每项研究都是观察一个样本，也就是一小群人，然后做出推断，也就是对所有人下结论。要判断这个结论站不站得住，问两个问题。第一，内部效度：这个结果可信吗？会不会是偏倚或混杂造成的？第二，外部效度：结果能不能用到研究对象以外，比如路上你的病人？一项只在医院急诊做的试验，可能做得很好，却不适合院前。研究者常常牺牲一个来换另一个，好让研究做得成。

slides.title: Experiments: RCT vs quasi-experimental
slides.body:
Who decides who gets the treatment?

  • Experimental: the researcher assigns it → can test cause
  • RCT: pure chance assigns; groups alike except the treatment
  • RCT downsides: slow, costly, strict entry → less generalizable
  • Quasi-experimental: assigned, but not truly at random
  • e.g. new device at some stations only → check group differences
slides.say: Quantitative studies, which count and measure, come in two families. The key question: who decides who gets the treatment? In an experimental study, the researcher decides, so it can test cause and effect. In a randomized controlled trial, or RCT, chance alone decides, so the groups end up alike except for the treatment. That gives strong internal validity, but it costs time and money, and strict entry rules can limit external validity. A quasi-experimental study assigns groups without true randomness, say a new device at some stations but not others. Then check whether the groups differ in age, sex, or severity.
slides.sayZh: 定量研究，也就是计数和测量的研究，分两大家族。关键问题是：谁决定谁接受治疗？实验研究由研究者决定，所以能检验因果。随机对照试验，也就是 RCT，完全由机会决定，所以两组除了治疗以外几乎一样，内部效度强；但它费时费钱，入组条件严格，可能限制外部效度。准实验研究分了组，但不是真随机，比如只给部分站点配新设备。这时要检查两组在年龄、性别、病情轻重上有没有差别。

slides.title: Observational studies: three designs
slides.body:
Cross-sectionalone snapshot in timeno cause and effect
Case-controlstart with the outcome, look backwho had the exposure?
Cohortstart with the exposure, follow forwardwho develops the outcome?

Nobody assigns the exposure, so these show association, not proof of cause.
slides.say: In observational studies, the researcher doesn't assign anything, only collects what happens. Take back injuries in paramedics. A cross-sectional study is a one-day survey: who has back pain, and who uses a power stretcher? It's a snapshot, so it can't show cause. A case-control study starts with the outcome: take paramedics who hurt their backs and others who didn't, then look back at what lifting equipment each used. A cohort study starts with the exposure: follow crews with and without power stretchers forward for years, and see who gets injured. So these designs show association, not proof of cause.
slides.sayZh: 观察研究里，研究者不分配任何东西，只收集发生的情况。拿救护员腰背受伤举例。横断面研究是一天的问卷：谁腰痛？谁用电动担架？这是快照，不能说明因果。病例对照研究从结局出发：找出伤了腰的救护员和没伤的，再回头查各自用过什么搬运设备。队列研究从暴露出发：跟踪有和没有电动担架的两组人，往后看几年，看谁受伤。所以这些设计只能显示关联，不能证明因果。

slides.q: Researchers find older adults who fell at home and similar adults who didn't. They then check records to compare how many sedating medications each group was taking. What kind of study is this?
slides.say: Time for a question. Researchers find older adults who fell at home and similar adults who didn't. Then they check records to compare how many sedating medications each group was taking. What kind of study is this? A, a randomized controlled trial. B, a cohort study. C, a case-control study. D, a cross-sectional study. Tap your answer.
slides.sayZh: 来做一道题。研究者找出在家里跌倒过的老人，以及条件相似、没跌倒过的老人，然后查记录，比较两组各在服用多少种镇静类药物。这是哪种研究？A 随机对照试验；B 队列研究；C 病例对照研究；D 横断面研究。点选你的答案。
slides.explain: The answer is C, a case-control study. The groups were formed by the outcome, a fall or no fall, and then the researchers looked back at an exposure, the medications. A cohort study works the other way: group people by their medications first, then follow them forward to see who falls. A cross-sectional study is a single snapshot, and an RCT needs the researcher to assign a treatment at random, which didn't happen here.
slides.explainZh: 答案是 C，病例对照研究。分组依据是结局（跌倒或没跌倒），然后研究者回头查暴露（用药）。队列研究正好相反：先按用药情况分组，再往后跟踪看谁跌倒。横断面研究是一次性快照；RCT 要由研究者随机分配治疗，这里并没有。

slides.title: Bias and confounding
slides.body:
Bias = a systematic error

  • Confounding: a third factor drives both treatment and outcome
  • e.g. the sickest get the helicopter, so its patients die more
  • Selection bias: who takes part differs from who doesn't
  • Misclassification: data put in the wrong group
  • Control it by randomizing, or with statistics if it was measured
slides.say: Bias is a systematic error: something in the study pushes the answer away from the truth. The most dangerous kind is confounding, when a third factor affects both who gets the treatment and how they do. Imagine a study finding that patients flown by helicopter die more often. But helicopters are sent to the sickest patients, so severity may be the real cause. Selection bias means the people who take part differ from those who don't, like a fatigue survey given only on day shifts. Misclassification puts data in the wrong group. Randomization controls confounding best; statistics help only if the factor was measured.
slides.sayZh: 偏倚是系统误差：研究中有某种东西，把答案推离了真相。最危险的是混杂，也就是某个第三因素既影响谁接受治疗，又影响结局。设想一项研究发现直升机转运的病人死亡更多，可直升机本来就派给最重的病人，真正的原因可能是病情轻重。选择偏倚是参加研究的人和没参加的人本身就不同，比如疲劳问卷只发给白班。错分偏倚是把数据归错了组。控制混杂最好的办法是随机分组；统计方法只有在那个因素被测量过时才帮得上忙。

slides.title: Chance: type I and type II errors
slides.body:
Random error = a difference that appears by chance alone.

ErrorThe study says…The truth is…
Type Ithere is a differencethere isn't
Type IIthere is no differencethere is one

Handled at the design stage: enrol enough patients for the size of difference you want to detect.
slides.say: Even a fair study can be fooled by chance. Flip a coin ten times and you might get seven heads, with nothing wrong with the coin. That's random error, and it causes two classic mistakes. A type one error says there's a difference when there isn't: a false alarm. A type two error says there's no difference when there is: a missed finding. Small studies easily miss real differences. So researchers calculate the sample size before they start: big enough to detect the difference they care about, but not so big that people are enrolled for no reason.
slides.sayZh: 就算研究公平，也可能被偶然骗到。抛十次硬币，可能出现七次正面，硬币本身却没问题。这就是随机误差，它造成两种经典错误。I 类错误：其实没有差异，却说有，也就是虚惊一场。II 类错误：其实有差异，却说没有，也就是漏掉了。小研究很容易漏掉真实的差异。所以研究者在开始前要计算样本量：够大，能测出他们关心的差异；又不能大到让人白白入组。

slides.title: Qualitative research: why and how
slides.body:
Words, not numbers: people's experience and its meaning

ApproachFocus
Descriptiveplain summary of an event or problem
Phenomenologylived experience and what it means
Grounded theorybuilds a new theory from participants
Ethnographya group's shared culture, by fieldwork

Judged by trustworthiness, not validity; researchers reflect on their own influence (reflexivity).
slides.say: Not every question is about numbers. Quantitative research asks how many, or whether something works. Qualitative research asks why and how, using words. For example: how do paramedics experience their first death notification? There are four common approaches. A descriptive study gives a plain summary. Phenomenology explores lived experience and its meaning. Grounded theory builds a new theory from what participants say. And ethnography studies a group's shared culture through fieldwork. Small samples are normal. These studies are judged by trustworthiness rather than validity, and good researchers practise reflexivity: openly asking how their own background shapes the study.
slides.sayZh: 不是每个问题都靠数字回答。定量研究问「有多少」或「有没有用」；定性研究用文字问「为什么」和「怎么样」。比如：救护员第一次通知家属死讯是什么感受？常见取向有四种。描述性研究给出平实的概括。现象学探究亲身经历及其意义。扎根理论从参与者的话里建立新理论。民族志通过实地观察研究一个群体共有的文化。样本小是正常的。这类研究看的是可信赖性而不是效度，好的研究者还会做反身性反思：公开思考自己的背景如何影响了研究。

slides.title: Asking a good question: FINER and PICO
slides.body:
FINERfeasible, interesting, novel, ethical, relevantis it worth asking?
PICOpopulation, intervention, comparison, outcomehow is it built?
Variablesindependent = what is changed; dependent = what is measuredprimary + secondary outcomes

Narrow entry criteria → a cleaner study, but lower external validity.
slides.say: Good studies start with good questions. FINER tests whether a question is worth asking: is it feasible, interesting, novel, ethical, and relevant? PICO gives it structure: population, intervention, comparison, outcome. For example: in adults with a wrist fracture, does a vacuum splint, compared with a board splint, reduce pain on arrival? The independent variable is what the researcher changes, the splint. The dependent variable is what's measured, the pain. The narrower the entry rules, say one age group with no other illnesses, the cleaner the result, but the less it fits your real patients.
slides.sayZh: 好研究从好问题开始。FINER 检验问题值不值得问：可行、有趣、新颖、合伦理、相关。PICO 给问题搭结构：人群、干预、对照、结局。比如：成人腕部骨折，用真空夹板对比木板夹板，到院时疼痛是否更轻？自变量是研究者改变的东西，也就是夹板；因变量是测量的东西，也就是疼痛。入组限制越窄，比如只收某个年龄段、没有其他疾病的人，结果越干净，但越不适合你真实的病人。

slides.title: Good data, and your PCR
slides.body:
• Reliability: the same result every time you measure
  • Validity: it measures what it claims to measure
  • Retrospective: existing records, like PCRs and dispatch data
  • Prospective: collected after the study starts → better control
  • If your service runs a study: forms complete and accurate

Research on people needs REB approval and, except in special cases, informed consent.
slides.say: Good research needs good data. Reliability means getting the same answer each time you measure. Validity means the tool measures what it claims to; a measure can be very consistent and still measure the wrong thing. A retrospective study uses existing records, like your patient care reports and dispatch times. It's quick, but data may be missing or unclear. A prospective study collects data after it starts, with trained staff and special forms, so it's better controlled. Any study on people needs approval from a research ethics board, or REB. If your service runs one, fill in the forms carefully: your accuracy protects the result.
slides.sayZh: 好研究需要好数据。信度是每次测量都得到同样的结果。效度是工具真的测到了它声称要测的东西；一项测量可以非常一致，却测错了对象。回顾性研究用现成的记录，比如你的病人照护报告和调度时间，快，但数据可能缺失或不清楚。前瞻性研究在研究开始后才收集，有培训过的人员和专用表格，控制得更好。凡是以人为对象的研究，都要经研究伦理委员会，也就是 REB 批准。如果你的服务在做研究，认真填好表格：你的准确就是在保护研究结果。

slides.title: P values: what they really mean
slides.body:
Null hypothesis: no difference→Calculate P→P < 0.05: reject the null
  • P = chance of a difference this big if there is really none
  • P > 0.05 means “no difference found”, not “the same”
  • Statistically significant ≠ clinically significant
  • Clinical significance: weighed by medical and system leaders
slides.say: Researchers start with a null hypothesis: no difference between the groups. Then they calculate a P value, from zero to one: how likely a difference this big, or bigger, would be if the null hypothesis were true. The usual cut-off is zero point zero five. Below it, they reject the null, and the result is statistically significant. Above it, they can only say they found no difference, which doesn't prove two treatments are equal. And statistical isn't clinical significance: a tiny difference may not matter to patients. Medical and system leaders weigh that, along with safety and cost.
slides.sayZh: 研究者先设零假设：两组没有差异。然后计算 P 值，介于零和一之间：如果零假设成立，出现这么大或更大差异的可能性有多大。常用界线是零点零五。低于它，就拒绝零假设，结果有统计学显著性。高于它，只能说没发现差异，这不能证明两种治疗一样。统计学显著也不等于临床显著：很小的差异可能对病人无关紧要。这要由医学界和系统领导权衡，同时考虑安全和成本。

slides.q: A colleague shows you a new emergency department study: a drug improved a blood test result, P = 0.03. He wants your crew to start using it next shift. What is the best response?
options: Agree: a P value under 0.05 proves it works for everyone
It's significant, but may not apply prehospital; changes go through medical direction
Ignore it: hospital studies never apply to paramedics
Wait for a P value above 0.05, which is stronger proof
slides.say: Let's try a PCP decision. A colleague shows you a new emergency department study: a drug improved a blood test result, with a P value of zero point zero three. He wants your crew to start using it next shift. What's the best response? A, agree; a P value under zero point zero five proves it works for everyone. B, it's significant, but it may not apply prehospital, and changes go through medical direction. C, ignore it; hospital studies never apply to paramedics. D, wait for a P value above zero point zero five, which is stronger proof. Tap your answer.
slides.sayZh: 来做一道 PCP 决策题。同事给你看一项新的急诊科研究：某药改善了一项血液检查结果，P 值为零点零三。他想让你们组下个班就开始用。最好的回应是什么？A 同意，P 值低于零点零五证明它对所有人有效；B 结果显著，但可能不适用于院前，改变做法要经过医疗指导；C 不理它，医院研究永远不适用于救护员；D 等 P 值高于零点零五的研究，那才是更强的证据。点选你的答案。
slides.explain: The answer is B. A P value under zero point zero five makes chance unlikely, but it doesn't prove the drug helps everyone, so A is wrong. A better blood test may not be a clinically important outcome, and a hospital study raises a question of external validity. Every drug you give as a PCP is delegated, so changes go through your medical director. C is too extreme: hospital research can apply if it fits. D gets P values backwards: a larger P value is weaker evidence of a difference.
slides.explainZh: 答案是 B。P 值低于零点零五说明偶然的可能性小，但不能证明这药对所有人有效，所以 A 错。血液检查变好不一定是有临床意义的结局，而医院研究搬到院前是外部效度问题。你作为 PCP 给的每一种药都是授权给你的，所以改变做法要经过医疗主任。C 太极端：医院研究如果契合，也可以适用。D 把 P 值弄反了：P 值越大，有差异的证据越弱。

slides.title: What the PCP actually does
slides.body:
• Knows why each protocol exists, and that it can change
  • Writes complete, accurate PCRs: they become research data
  • Completes study forms fully when the service runs a trial
  • Reads the methods first: design, groups, who was included
  • Takes questions to medical direction; no solo practice changes
slides.say: What does this mean for a working PCP? First, protocols are built on evidence, and they change when better evidence arrives. Second, your patient care reports matter beyond the call. Retrospective studies are built from them, so a missing time or a vague note can weaken research years later. Third, if your service runs a study, learn its forms and complete them fully. Fourth, when you read a paper, go to the methods: what design, which groups, who was included? Fifth, if a study makes you question a protocol, take it to medical direction. Push for change through the system, not alone on a call.
slides.sayZh: 这对在职 PCP 意味着什么？第一，流程建立在证据上，有了更好的证据就会改。第二，你的病人照护报告在出车之后仍然重要：回顾性研究就是用它们做的，少一个时间、一句含糊的记录，可能在多年后削弱一项研究。第三，服务在做研究时，学会它的表格并填完整。第四，读论文直接看方法部分：什么设计、哪些组、纳入了谁？第五，如果某项研究让你质疑某条流程，提交给医疗指导。推动改变要通过系统，而不是在出车时自己改。

slides.title: New for you as a PCP: watch out for
slides.body:
• Association is not cause: be careful with observational studies
  • “No significant difference” doesn't mean “equally good”
  • Significant isn't always important to patients
  • A hospital or ED study may not fit the back of an ambulance
  • Narrow entry rules: were those patients like yours?
  • Small study + “no difference” → think type II error
slides.say: Here are the traps to watch for. One: an observational study shows association, not cause, so ask what else could explain the link. Two: no significant difference doesn't mean equally good. Three: a statistically significant result may be too small to matter. Four: a hospital or emergency department study may not fit prehospital care; that's external validity. Five: check who was allowed in. If older or sicker patients were excluded, the results may not fit yours. Six: when a small study finds no difference, think type two error. It may have been too small to see one.
slides.sayZh: 这些陷阱要注意。一，观察研究显示的是关联，不是因果，问问还有什么能解释这个联系。二，没有显著差异，不代表一样好。三，统计学显著的结果，可能小到没有意义。四，医院或急诊的研究未必适合院前，这是外部效度问题。五，看清允许谁入组；如果排除了老人或重病人，结果可能不适合你的病人。六，小研究得出没有差异时，想想 II 类错误：可能只是太小，看不出来。

slides.title: Three things to remember
slides.body:
1. Evidence + expertise + experience; protocols change with evidence
  2. Design sets what a study can prove: RCT tests cause; observational shows association
  3. P < 0.05 = statistically significant, not automatically clinically important

Next: using evidence, quality improvement and patient safety
slides.say: Let's wrap up with three things to remember. One: good care combines research evidence with your expertise and experience, and protocols change when the evidence does. Two: the design tells you what a study can prove. A randomized controlled trial can test cause and effect; observational designs show association. Three: a P value under zero point zero five means statistically significant, not automatically important to patients, and a P value above it doesn't prove two treatments are the same. Next lesson: finding and appraising evidence, then quality improvement and patient safety. If anything was unclear, tap Ask. See you next class.
slides.sayZh: 收尾三句话。一，好的照护是把研究证据和你的专长、经验结合起来，证据变了，流程也会变。二，设计决定了研究能证明什么：随机对照试验能检验因果，观察设计只显示关联。三，P 值低于零点零五叫统计学显著，不一定对病人重要；P 值高于它，也不能证明两种治疗一样。下节课：查找和评价证据，然后是质量改进和患者安全。有不懂的点「Ask」。下节课见。
